Listeriosis Class Action

By: Kate Barry | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Six years after South Africa's listeriosis outbreak ended the ill effects are still being felt - and a thousand victims still wait for compensation.

Unique Selling Point:
Interviews with the scientists who have proved through extensive genetic sequencing that the listeriosis outbreak originated from the Enterprise Factory in Polokwane.
Interviews with some of the claimants who suffered damage as a result of contracting listeriosis. (Cerebral palsy in children, loss of a breadwinner etc)
Interviews with the specialist lawyers who are representing the claimants in their class action against Enterprise Foods and holding company Tiger Brands.

Summary:
Between Nov 2016 and 2018 Tiger Brands produced, distributed and supplied ready-to-eat meat products (particularly colony) contaminated with listeriosis. The food poisoning resulted in the deaths of 216 people. However, many more people suffered harm (about 1000) and the effects are still being felt today.
An article published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that because of the high prevalence of HIV in South Africa, listeriosis caused disproportionate cases of illness in pregnant girls and women (465) and HIV infected persons. Of the 465 pregnancy cases, 405 were neonates/newborn babies, as listeriosis can be transmitted from mother to foetus.
In 2018 the Gauteng High Court certified Richard Spoor Inc and LHL Attorneys Inc as class attorneys in a class action against Tiger Brands. The claim is based on the findings of the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD). The NICD conducted an investigation into the listeriosis outbreak, which included a microbiological investigation.

Further information:
The NICD used various whole genome sequencing methods and detected various STs
during the outbreak. Around 93% of the sequenced listeriosis cases during the outbreak
were classified as sequence type 6 (ST6). The ST6 strain was also found at the Tiger
Brands Polokwane facility and in Tiger Brands’ products, including polony. The ST6 strain was not found at any other location or facility during the outbreak period except the Polokwane facility.
despite clear evidence of Tiger Brands culpability,
they have dragged their feet and exploited every legal loophole available to delay the
resolution of this matter.

Script:


LISTERIOSIS CLASS ACTION


V/O: In 2017, long before the pandemic changed our lives, South Africa faced another public health crisis.

Montlha: She got it from me while I was pregnant.

VO Listeriosis – a food-borne disease - caused illness and death across the country.

Thami This was the largest and deadliest outbreak of listeria ever recorded in world history.

VO Over a thousand people were infected and 218 people died.

CEO: There is no direct link with the deaths to our products. (CB 2018)

VO But the battle for justice is ongoing.

FADE TO BLACK

Link: This is the beginning of a journey that could take us to any province in the country, but it’s taking us to Bloemfontein. We’re speaking to one of the victims of a national outbreak of a disease that was brought under control six years ago, but one from which the victims are still suffering.

V/O: Mother of three Annelize le Roux was told she wouldn’t conceive again, so was overjoyed in February 2018 when her gynaecologist said she was expecting another boy.

Annelize: He showed me on the sonar that everything is fine, everything looks good. And he just mentioned that this little baby is very busy. He’s very busy.

V/O: But just a few days later she was rushed to hospital with a high fever.

Annelize: Then I got the devastating news that my baby is dead. There is no heartbeat anymore.


Annelize: It didn’t make sense at that stage because I know it was a miracle.

VO Blood tests confirmed that Annelize had listeriosis, which had infected her unborn baby. Over 140 mothers suffered stillbirths and miscarriages, but these were not factored into the final death toll.

Link: This is a pathogen that targets the weak and the vulnerable. So, people living with a compromised immune system. Almost half of the cases were associated with pregnancy, and the overwhelming majority of the dead were either unborn children or infants infected in utero or during birth.

V/O: Next, we go north to Limpopo, to meet seven-year-old Theto, living with the effects of listeriosis contracted in the womb. Her mother Montlha Ngobeni was told her new-born had hydrocephalus.

Montlha: They found out there is water accumulating in the brain. Very painful. That’s when the painful journey began.

Montlha: After that they told me they’re gonna take her to theatre for an operation, that’s when reality kicks.

Govan: How old was she?

Montlha: Eighteen days.

V/O: Doctors inserted a shunt in Theto’s head to drain the excess fluid. She’s had six operations in her short life to replace the shunt.

Montlha: The medical aid ended up being exhausted. And for Theto, for her six operations its more than 600 000. We had a lot of debts. We are not coping. Absolutely not coping.

V/O: Montlha says she knows exactly where she contracted listeriosis. Craving polony and viennas during her pregnancy, she was a regular customer at Enterprise in Polokwane.

Monthla: I loved Enterprise food. I loved those ready to eat foods. I went to support this big business to grow so that I can kill my baby.

V/O: Having once worked in a food factory, Annelize took samples from her own fridge - including Enterprise polony - and gave them to health officials.

Annelize I could manage to take a photograph of the sell-by date of the batch numbers or whatever information that was still on the products.

Govan: Were you able to prove which product you contracted the listeriosis from?

Annelise: The NICD contact me. They told me the information I gave them played a crucial part in the investigation. And they could actually trace the source. I always felt like my son, he can’t just die for nothing.

[TRANSITION]

VO: In 2018, we brought you the story of the hunt for the source of the listeriosis outbreak.
LINK: This is where the real detective work was done – in a laboratory using whole genome sequencing.
VO: Dr Juno Thomas from the National Institute for Communicable Diseases, led the team that used cutting-edge DNA analysis to identify the killer bacteria.

Juno: All our human cases we’ve done this whole genome sequencing on to date, 91% of them belong to a single strain, and that’s our outbreak strain.

V/O: The outbreak strain ST6 was eventually traced to polony produced in the Enterprise factory in Polokwane.

Juno: In total over 340 samples were taken. 104 yielded Listeria monocytogenes – that’s almost 30%.

LINK: But our scientists went a step further: through high-resolution analysis they were able to match the strain found in the humans, to the strain found in the meat products, to the strain found in the factory at Polokwane.

Juno: Over 90% of patients developed disease from the outbreak strain ST6. Now we have evidence from the factory that both the direct environment was contaminated with ST6 as well as polony products that were about to be shipped out to the retail industry.

Link: So, this is ground zero. Scientists proved that the listeriosis outbreak started here at this factory. The ST6 strain of listeria responsible for the vast majority of infections was not found at any other location or facility except right here in Polokwane.

VO Enterprise was owned by Tiger Brands. The company agreed that ST6 contaminated products from its factory probably infected some people but denied that it caused the outbreak. Former CEO Lawrence MacDougall:

CEO: There is no direct link with the deaths to our products that we’re aware of at this point. Nothing.

V/O: The Polokwane factory was closed and within weeks the outbreak was over. But to this day, the victims are fighting for compensation.

V/O: Richard Spoor Incorporated is representing over 800 claimants in a class action against Tiger Brands.

Thami: A class action in a nutshell allows a group of representatives to bring a case on behalf of everyone who has suffered the same objective harm stemming from the same source essentially.

V/O: Thami Malusi is leading the team of attorneys.

Thami: We felt that it’s a right case for us and that the people that approached us desperately needed our expertise.

V/O: Thami works closely with his colleague Zeenat Emmamally.

Zeenat: What we’re looking for primarily is justice and compensation for those that suffered harm as a result of consuming Tiger Brands products. We’ve got claimants who contracted listeriosis as adults and lost their ability to walk. We have women who suffered stillbirths and they’re dealing with the psychological impact to this day. And what I think is perhaps most devastating is neonates - infants younger than 28 days - this is the most affected age group, approximately 400 children who survived listeriosis and who are suffering from conditions now like permanent brain damage, constant seizures and other developmental issues.

VO In court papers, Tiger Brands denies all these allegations. To assist with this case, the team brought in Bill Marler, the most prominent foodborne illness lawyer in America.

Govan: What did you find significant about the South African outbreak?

Bill: Frankly, the good thing is that you know the NICD did a spectacular job. They found positive listeria samples in the plant, that were an absolute genetic match to the ill and the dead in South Africa. And that’s really super important to understand that there is absolutely, unequivocally no question that Tiger Brands was the source of this outbreak.

Link: The NICD has declined an interview saying that they will not be commenting publicly at this time. However, their research has been reviewed by international experts at the Centers for Disease Control in America.

Bill: I retained some of the best experts on epidemiology and listeriosis in the world. Bar none. They have absolute unequivocal scientific backing.

Link: Tiger Brands declined an interview with Carte Blanche 6 years ago, and they’re declining an interview now. In a letter to us they say:
“We are saddened by the impact Listeriosis had and continues to have on the lives of the victims and are committed to resolving the class action lawsuit in the shortest possible time.”
They also say they their legal team is “preparing for trial where liability will be determined by the Court.”
So, there’s clearly no intention to settle here.

VO Despite this commitment to a speedy resolution, the victims are still waiting. The class action was certified six years ago - but has faced one delay after another.

Thami: If we were dealing with a reasonable defendant, this case should have been long settled. The issue here is that Tiger Brands has utilized just about every legal technicality available to them to delay this case.

Nthabiseng: Let me see your toy Onkarabile. Thank you.

V/O: In the meantime, victims like Nthabiseng Ramanamane are struggling to cope.
She too contracted listeriosis during pregnancy; her son, Onkarabile was born at 31 weeks with cerebral palsy.

Nthabiseng: Looking at my child, it is a constant reminder of Enterprise and Tiger Brands and everything.

V/O: She’s doing her PhD in mechanical engineering at UNISA but can only visit the lab once a week. Onkarabile - now aged 7 - is totally dependent on his mom.

Nthabiseng: When he was six months, he had his first shunt. So that was his first operation. But that was not the last operation for him.

Govan: How many operations has he had?

Nthabiseng: He had his shunt replaced in 2022. And afterwards we had a pack, he is feeding through the stomach.

V/O: Onkarabile has already had one operation for the hip dislocation caused by his condition. He’s scheduled for another next year. As a single parent Nthabiseng is struggling to cope financially with her son’s needs: a special diet, adult diapers, medical bills.

Nthabiseng: As you can see, I’m balancing him, I’m balancing his head, the entire body. So, it means that Onkarabile is a dependent, possibly for the rest of his life.

Thami: If you take a case like that, we can estimate that to be anything between 15 and 20 million rands. And if you multiply that by the number of kids that we have, you start to get closer to the billion-rand mark.

Bill: If the Tiger Brands outbreak had happened in the United States, Tiger Brands would be facing at least $1 billion in damages.

Govan: A billion?

Bill: A billion US dollars in damages. If this case goes to court, the court will find them liable. Period.

VO Tiger Brands has liability insurance with SHA Risk Specialists, a division of Santam.

Zeenat: They are the ones who have taken over the litigation on behalf of Tiger Brands, and it would be them who would be liable to pay this amount out.

VO According to Tiger Brands, Santam appointed experts to review the scientific research six months ago. The review is ongoing. Santam has nothing to add to Tiger Brands’ statement, saying it would be inappropriate to comment at this stage.

[ONSCREEN] We have nothing to add to the statement issued by Tiger Brands (as our insured) and consider it inappropriate to respond to the questions posed, in light of the ongoing litigation.

Govan: What has been your opinion of the legal strategy employed by the insurers over the last six years?

Thami: Delay. Because that allows them to make money off the interest that is earned by the money reserved for this eventuality.

Bill: It’s ridiculous! Tiger Brands should be forcing the insurance company to do the right thing by their customers.

Annelise: It feels like a lack of integrity; a lack of morality.

V/O: But for now, the victims will have to make do with media statements.

Govan: Tiger Brands says it is saddened by the impact which listeriosis has had and continues to have on the lives of the victims.

Montlha: Those are liars. They’re not saddened by anything. If they were saddened, they would have done the right thing a long time ago. This is seven years now.

VO Despite this commitment to a speedy resolution, the victims are still waiting. The class action was certified six years ago - but has faced one delay after another. Thami: If we were dealing with a reasonable defendant, this case should have been long settled. The issue here is that Tiger Brands has utilized just about every legal technicality available to them to delay this case. Nthabiseng: Let me see your toy Onkarabile. Thank you. V/O: In the meantime, victims like Nthabiseng Ramanamane are struggling to cope. She too contracted listeriosis during pregnancy; her son, Onkarabile was born at 31 weeks with cerebral palsy. Nthabiseng: Looking at my child, it is a constant reminder of Enterprise and Tiger Brands and everything. V/O: She’s doing her PhD in mechanical engineering at UNISA but can only visit the lab once a week. Onkarabile - now aged 7 - is totally dependent on his mom. Nthabiseng: When he was six months, he had his first shunt. So that was his first operation. But that was not the last operation for him. Govan: How many operations has he had? Nthabiseng: He had his shunt replaced in 2022. And afterwards we had a pack, he is feeding through the stomach. V/O: Onkarabile has already had one operation for the hip dislocation caused by his condition. He’s scheduled for another next year. As a single parent Nthabiseng is struggling to cope financially with her son’s needs: a special diet, adult diapers, medical bills. Nthabiseng: As you can see, I’m balancing him, I’m balancing his head, the entire body. So, it means that Onkarabile is a dependent, possibly for the rest of his life. Thami: If you take a case like that, we can estimate that to be anything between 15 and 20 million rands. And if you multiply that by the number of kids that we have, you start to get closer to the billion-rand mark. Bill: If the Tiger Brands outbreak had happened in the United States, Tiger Brands would be facing at least $1 billion in damages. Govan: A billion? Bill: A billion US dollars in damages. If this case goes to court, the court will find them liable. Period. VO Tiger Brands has liability insurance with SHA Risk Specialists, a division of Santam. Zeenat: They are the ones who have taken over the litigation on behalf of Tiger Brands, and it would be them who would be liable to pay this amount out. VO According to Tiger Brands, Santam appointed experts to review the scientific research six months ago. The review is ongoing. Santam has nothing to add to Tiger Brands’ statement, saying it would be inappropriate to comment at this stage. [ONSCREEN] We have nothing to add to the statement issued by Tiger Brands (as our insured) and consider it inappropriate to respond to the questions posed, in light of the ongoing litigation. Govan: What has been your opinion of the legal strategy employed by the insurers over the last six years? Thami: Delay. Because that allows them to make money off the interest that is earned by the money reserved for this eventuality. Bill: It’s ridiculous! Tiger Brands should be forcing the insurance company to do the right thing by their customers. Annelise: It feels like a lack of integrity; a lack of morality. V/O: But for now, the victims will have to make do with media statements. Govan: Tiger Brands says it is saddened by the impact which listeriosis has had and continues to have on the lives of the victims. Montlha: Those are liars. They’re not saddened by anything. If they were saddened, they would have done the right thing a long time ago. This is seven years now.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Six years after South Africa's listeriosis outbreak ended the ill effects are still being felt - and a thousand victims still wait for compensation.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Interviews with the scientists who have proved through extensive genetic sequencing that the listeriosis outbreak originated from the Enterprise Factory in Polokwane. Interviews with some of the claimants who suffered damage as a result of contracting listeriosis. (Cerebral palsy in children, loss of a breadwinner etc) Interviews with the specialist lawyers who are representing the claimants in their class action against Enterprise Foods and holding company Tiger Brands.
metadata.Summary: Between Nov 2016 and 2018 Tiger Brands produced, distributed and supplied ready-to-eat meat products (particularly colony) contaminated with listeriosis. The food poisoning resulted in the deaths of 216 people. However, many more people suffered harm (about 1000) and the effects are still being felt today. An article published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that because of the high prevalence of HIV in South Africa, listeriosis caused disproportionate cases of illness in pregnant girls and women (465) and HIV infected persons. Of the 465 pregnancy cases, 405 were neonates/newborn babies, as listeriosis can be transmitted from mother to foetus. In 2018 the Gauteng High Court certified Richard Spoor Inc and LHL Attorneys Inc as class attorneys in a class action against Tiger Brands. The claim is based on the findings of the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD). The NICD conducted an investigation into the listeriosis outbreak, which included a microbiological investigation.
metadata.Further information: The NICD used various whole genome sequencing methods and detected various STs during the outbreak. Around 93% of the sequenced listeriosis cases during the outbreak were classified as sequence type 6 (ST6). The ST6 strain was also found at the Tiger Brands Polokwane facility and in Tiger Brands’ products, including polony. The ST6 strain was not found at any other location or facility during the outbreak period except the Polokwane facility. despite clear evidence of Tiger Brands culpability, they have dragged their feet and exploited every legal loophole available to delay the resolution of this matter.
